html:
Erik Erikson framed lifespan development as a series of eight sequential "psychosocial crises." At each turning point the individual negotiates a tension between two opposing pulls-e.g., trust vs mistrust-within a specific social arena. Successful resolution does not eliminate the negative pole; it integrates it, yielding a new adaptive strength or "basic virtue" that equips the person for later, more complex challenges. Because each stage builds on the previous ones, early setbacks can echo forward, yet growth always remains possible through later corrective experience. The relationships in this account are summarized schematically (Figure).

Crises

Trust vs Mistrust (birth -  18 months). The infant’s primary task is to decide whether the world is reliably responsive to its basic needs. Consistent caregiving-feeding when hungry, soothing when distressed-fosters a foundational sense that external reality can be counted on and that one’s own signals matter. From this successful balancing act emerges hope: the nascent confidence to reach out and engage a world that may, ultimately, provide for one’s needs. Persistent neglect or unpredictability tips the scale toward mistrust, seeding suspicion and withdrawal.

Autonomy vs Shame & Doubt ( 18 months - 3 years). Mobility and language usher in new possibilities for self-control: toddlers want to say "No!" and do things "by myself." Supportive scaffolding-allowing choice within safe limits-cultivates a felt sense of autonomy and the virtue of will: the capacity to act with self-directed intention. Overly harsh criticism or intrusive control can instead breed shame and doubt, leaving the child hesitant about their own impulses and abilities.

Initiative vs Guilt ( 3 - 6 years). As imagination and social play explode, children test out roles: pirate, parent, builder. When caregivers and peers acknowledge these self-generated enterprises, initiative flourishes, crystallizing as purpose: the courage to envisage and pursue valued goals. If the child is consistently made to feel that desires are foolish or morally suspect, excessive guilt dampens spontaneity and aspiration.

Industry vs Inferiority ( 6 - 11 years). School and peer comparison shift the arena to culturally valued skills-reading, calculating, teamwork. Mastery experiences reinforce industriousness and elicit competence: a belief in one’s ability to methodically produce desired outcomes. Continual failure, ridicule, or unattainable standards foster a gnawing sense of inferiority that can undermine future achievement motivation.

Identity vs Role Confusion (adolescence). Puberty and abstract thought propel the search for a coherent self: "Who am I, and what do I stand for?" Successful synthesis of past identifications, future aspirations, and societal feedback yields fidelity: the capacity to commit to values, relationships, and an emerging life trajectory while tolerating internal contradictions. When exploration is stifled or fragmented, role confusion breeds chronic uncertainty and susceptibility to external definition.

Intimacy vs Isolation (young adulthood). Having defined a self, the individual now seeks genuine partnership that entails mutual vulnerability without losing personal boundaries. Achieving true intimacy generates the virtue of love: the ability to fuse identities yet remain whole. Failure-through fear of engulfment or of rejection-can leave one isolated, emotionally guarded, or prone to superficial connections.

Generativity vs Stagnation (mid-adulthood). Attention turns outward to nurturing the next generation or contributing lasting work-child-rearing, mentoring, civic projects, innovation. When effort flows into enterprises that outlive the self, care emerges: a widening concern for society’s continuity. Absent such engagement, stagnation and self-absorption may dominate, accompanied by a sense of life’s inertia.

Integrity vs Despair (late adulthood). Confronting finitude, the elder reviews life’s narrative. If earlier crises were navigated well enough to weave a coherent, meaningful story-accepting both triumphs and failures-integrity prevails, fostering the virtue of wisdom: a detached yet compassionate grasp of life’s complexity and mortality. If regret and unintegrated loss overshadow reflection, despair can set in, tinged by bitterness and fear of death.

Erikson stressed that each crisis is re-visited in subtler forms across later phases-trust inside intimacy, autonomy inside generativity-making development a lifelong, recursive dialogue between self and society. Environments that pose realistic challenges while offering support maximize the odds of resolving each tension on the growth-promoting side, enriching the individual’s repertoire of psychological strengths. This schematic maps the article’s main ideas (Figure).
